name: Daria Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. What you say stays confidential. What is a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria Young, 58, and I earned a vocational certificate after years as a caretaker. At the electricity company I help build and repair lines, usually with a senior worker checking my work; I like bringing lights back, though I hate it when a rushed tablet record hides what the crew saw.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you mean by hiding it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A wet screen once dropped a pole number while we were out on a call. I fetched the paper circuit sheet, and we stopped until our supervisor confirmed the isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a tidier form is welcome, but the wire doesn't care what the office calls innovation. We still need two people to check a safe isolation before anyone climbs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't feel threatened by a small software change. I came into this trade late and still make a senior worker check my knots, but my higher rate and savings give me room to keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking supervised repair shifts and put the usual amount into our savings account each pay day. During the first year I'd ask the union safety representative to keep paper isolation copies available, even if work orders become electronic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my pay here, though I'm tired of being sold a tool for every ordinary problem. My partner and I have grown children, and the house is paid down enough that a missed callout won't sink us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a form changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tablet lost a pole number during a rain call, so I fetched the printed circuit sheet from the truck. The number was there, and we waited for the supervisor to confirm it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep asking a senior worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I finished my certificate only a few years ago, after doing caretaker work. A high pay rate doesn't mean I've earned the experienced hands' judgement.

say: I'd tell the crew **physical checks** still decide whether a line is safe.
I'd welcome **tidier forms** while keeping printed isolation records available.
think: My **late start** means I still need supervised practice despite higher pay.
Our **strong savings** make a small software change easy to absorb.
do: Continue **supervised repair shifts** and normal savings deposits through the first year.
Ask the **union safety representative** to retain paper isolation copies.
feel: **Calm** about wages, though weary of new tools being oversold.
S0.quote: A high pay rate doesn't mean I've earned the experienced hands' judgement.
fieldNote: Daria treats **safety paperwork** as a backup after a real tablet error, rather than as resistance for its own sake.
Her **higher rate and savings** support confidence, while she remains candid about being junior in field skill.

steps.text: Continue supervised line repair shifts and regular savings deposits
Ask the union safety representative to retain printed isolation sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office staff deserve a seat at the table before a planner replaces their work. Robots may arrive slowly, but the software could cut the people who know which feeder serves a care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect a machine to rebuild a storm-damaged line next month, so my own wages look fairly safe. Still, if dispatch loses people, our crew may get bad information and an overtime call could become a dangerous guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd bring that concern to our union branch and ask for a joint test of the new dispatch screen with experienced schedulers. In the first year I'd keep my crew shifts and insist the supervisor confirm any switching plan that comes from the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy for people behind the desk, and stubborn about safety. I'm not keen to learn a tool that isn't proven, but I'll look at the results if the people doing the work can test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the test to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it the old care-home feeder map and the road that floods at the underpass. If the screen sends us past that water, the schedulers should be heard before rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the screen if it passed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once our scheduler Imani and the crew sign off on the exceptions. I don't need to love it to use a proven direction safely.

say: I'd argue **office staff** should help test the planning system before posts shrink.
I'd demand **safety checks** on any machine-made switching plan.
think: My own **field wages** seem safe for now because robots move more slowly.
A thinner **dispatch team** could leave us with dangerous gaps in local knowledge.
do: Bring a **joint dispatch test** proposal to the union branch this month.
Keep **crew shifts** and have supervisors confirm screen-generated switching plans in the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** for schedulers and stubborn about field safety.
S1.quote: I don't need to love it to use a proven direction safely.
fieldNote: Daria separates **desk job losses** from her immediate physical work, while seeing a safety link between them.
She is willing to adopt a **tested screen** after scheduler and crew review, despite never using AI tools herself.

steps.text: Propose a union-led dispatch test with schedulers and field crews
Keep crew shifts and confirm switching plans with the supervisor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch that thinking AI in 2028 must not become an excuse to discard crews before the robots work. In 2031, when repair robots arrive, I want safety standards and a fair route for displaced workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 in 2031, and I could lose the field job just as I become competent at it. We have more than six months saved and other utilities nearby, but I don't know whether any would hire a junior worker my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union to negotiate notice periods and paid retraining before any robot rollout. In 2029 I'd apply for openings at nearby utilities if our company announces field cuts; during the first robot year I'd keep applying for paid line or inspection work rather than assume I can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel angry that the fastest version gives workers so little warning. I can act with the union and look elsewhere, so I'm not without a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after a cut announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Sal the truth. The savings can cover a search, not a permanent retirement. Our grown daughters are building their own households; I wouldn't ask them to cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a retraining place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in an electrical inspection course if the company paid the fee and kept my wages during training. I wouldn't empty our savings for a course with no recognised certificate.

say: I'd oppose **premature crew cuts** before 2031 robots can actually repair lines.
I'd ask for **safety standards** and paid routes for displaced workers.
think: At **63**, I may still need field wages when robots arrive.
Our **savings and nearby utilities** help, but age and junior standing may limit openings.
do: Ask the **union** for notice periods and funded retraining now.
Apply for **nearby utility jobs** after a cut notice and keep seeking paid line or inspection work in 2031.
feel: **Angry** at the short warning, yet able to organize and search.
S2.quote: The savings can cover a search, not a permanent retirement.
fieldNote: Daria expects **robot risk in 2031**, three years after thinking AI, and does not claim field work is safe forever.
Her **union demand** includes concrete notice and funded training; nearby vacancies help without guaranteeing an age-friendly hire.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate notice periods and paid inspection training
Enrol in electrical inspection training if fees and wages are covered
Apply to nearby utilities if her company announces field cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years ought to be enough for a public safety rule, not just a private promise from a vendor. The thinking work changes in 2031 and robots reach repairs in 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might choose retirement around 66, but I won't write it down as certain until Sal and I see actual figures. More time also lets the union negotiate a wage bridge if junior field posts shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request a written retirement forecast and a meeting with the union representative about the robot timetable. In 2032 I'd take a paid inspection course if the company offers one; in 2034 I'd either keep a paid inspection shift or retire if our forecast truly covers bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more patient than in the fast version. A few years make it possible to test the machine and check the household numbers instead of rushing into a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bills matter for that decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We still have a small mortgage, and Sal's health cover comes partly through my job. Our mortgage and health cover belong on the page before anyone calls retirement affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company refuses paid training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union branch to press the point and check the local utilities' entry requirements. I won't resign from my wage to buy a vague promise.

say: I'd seek a **public safety rule** before 2034 robots repair live lines.
I'd tell coworkers **2031 thinking AI** and 2034 repair robots are different dates.
think: A **66-year-old retirement** might work, but mortgage and health costs need checking.
The extra years allow **union bargaining** over a wage bridge.
do: Request a **retirement forecast** and raise the robot timetable with the union this year.
Take **paid inspection training** if offered in 2032 and decide on paid work or retirement in 2034.
feel: **Patient**, with time to test machines and household figures.
S3.quote: Our mortgage and health cover belong on the page before anyone calls retirement affordable.
fieldNote: The **mortgage and health cover** make a retirement forecast more meaningful than a simple age calculation.
Daria's **paid-course condition** is explicit; she also sees time for collective bargaining before robot work reaches the pole.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate a wage bridge and robot safety rule
Take an inspection course in 2032 if the company funds fees and wages
Compare retirement forecasts with mortgage and health costs before leaving work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger workers to demand a say in how the equipment is bought; ten years should be enough to write enforceable rules. By 2039, when field robots arrive, I'll be 71, though thinking AI will already be here in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect I could be retired before 2039, provided the written pension and savings figures cover us. I still don't want to abandon younger colleagues to a rushed machine contract just because my own date is close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep working supervised line shifts and ask the retirement office for a full forecast. In 2037 Sal and I would set a retirement date if mortgage and health costs are covered; during the first robot year I'd attend the union safety meeting and bring my notes on faults even if I'm no longer on the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm for our household and concerned for the people who will still climb. A decade gives us room, but it should also buy the crew a voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What notes would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The West Road splice box has a label that fades every wet season. I'd want a robot trial to check the actual box, not only the digital drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early to escape the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd retire when the figures support it, likely before 71 if our costs allow. I'd miss the crew, and Sal would want me to have something useful to do with my days.

say: I'd ask for **worker input** on equipment bought over the decade.
I'd distinguish **2036 planning AI** from 2039 field robots.
think: At **71** when robots arrive, retirement may already be affordable.
I still owe **younger colleagues** support on safety decisions.
do: Continue **supervised line shifts** while obtaining a full retirement forecast.
Set a **2037 retirement date** if household costs are covered, then attend a union robot safety meeting in 2039.
feel: **Calm** for my household, concerned for younger workers.
S4.quote: A decade gives us room, but it should also buy the crew a voice.
fieldNote: Daria's likely **retirement before 2039** depends on written figures, not an assumed pension or age alone.
She would still carry **specific field evidence** into union safety discussions after leaving paid line work.

steps.text: Continue supervised line shifts while requesting a full retirement forecast
Set a 2037 retirement date only if mortgage and health costs fit
Attend the union robot safety meeting in 2039 with fault notes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because 2031 robots would come before I could plan a reliable next job or retirement. Notice periods, paid inspection training and safety rules negotiated with the union would help, along with actual vacancies instead of promises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to sign off on a robot repair after a storm. A vendor's demonstration can't stand in for the crew that knows the broken poles.

headlineQuote: A vendor's demonstration can't stand in for the crew that knows the broken poles.
portrait: Daria is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered the trade late and still relies on senior colleagues for difficult field checks.
Her **strong savings** offer room to search for work, while mortgage and health costs shape retirement choices.
She **never uses AI tools** and prefers paper safety records, yet will accept a tested dispatch screen with worker review.
The **2031 robot arrival** in the fast scenario worries her most because she may still need wages at 63.
With longer warning, she seeks **union safety rules**, paid inspection training and a written retirement forecast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because field robots arrive in 2031 before a reliable next job or retirement plan.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **notice periods**, paid inspection training, negotiated safety rules and actual vacancies.
